description: Every piece of database logic is built from the same skeleton: DECLARE, BEGIN, EXCEPTION, END. Variables, SELECT INTO, and calling your own procedures and functions.

screens.body: Every block of database code — anonymous or stored — has the same skeleton. DECLARE (optional): where variables are born. BEGIN (required): where the work happens. EXCEPTION (optional): where errors get caught. END: the full stop. Learn this shape once and you can read any database program.

check.question: The four sections of a database block, in order:

code.snippet:
DECLARE
  -- variables go here (optional)
BEGIN
  -- the work goes here (required)
EXCEPTION
  -- error handling goes here (optional)
END;

screens.heading: One block, three (plus one) sections
screens.keyPoint: DECLARE → BEGIN → EXCEPTION → END. Same skeleton every time.

screens.body: Variables are declared up top with a name, a type, and an optional starting value. The types mirror column types: NUMBER, VARCHAR2(50), DATE, BOOLEAN. The := is assignment — it sets the value right now. Think of DECLARE as laying out your tools before you start working.

check.question: In v_name VARCHAR2(50) := 'Roli', what does := do?

screens.heading: DECLARE: your variables live here

screens.body: Here's a trick you'll love: v_price products.price%TYPE means 'give this variable whatever type the price column has.' If someone later changes the column from NUMBER(8,2) to NUMBER(10,2), your variable follows automatically — no hunting through code to fix types. %ROWTYPE goes further: one variable shaped like an entire row.

options: Whatever type the price column currently has
check.question: v_price products.price%TYPE gives v_price…

screens.heading: %TYPE: steal the column's type
screens.keyPoint: %TYPE anchors your variable to the column — schema changes can't break it.

screens.body: BEGIN is where things happen. The star move: SELECT ... INTO. It runs a query and pours the single result row straight into your variables. One catch — it must return exactly ONE row. Zero rows or two rows? That's an error (and topic 4 will teach you to catch it).

options: It pours one result row into your variables
check.question: SELECT price INTO v_price does what?

screens.heading: BEGIN: SELECT INTO, the star move
screens.keyPoint: SELECT ... INTO pulls exactly one row into variables.

screens.body: You don't have to build everything yourself. Built-in functions do the boring work: SYSDATE (right now), UPPER/LOWER (case), LENGTH, NVL (swap NULL for a fallback). Built-in procedures like DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE print while you debug. Using them is the norm, not cheating — it's why they exist.

options: Replace a NULL with a fallback value
check.question: NVL(price, 0) will…

code.snippet:
SELECT UPPER(name), NVL(price, 0)
FROM products;

-- SYSDATE: the database's current date and time
-- LENGTH('hello') = 5

screens.heading: Built-ins: free tools
screens.keyPoint: SYSDATE, UPPER, NVL, LENGTH — use them, that's what they're for.

screens.body: Blocks can call the executable units from last topic. Call a procedure to DO something; call a function inside an expression to COMPUTE something. Procedures are statements on their own line. Functions return a value, so they show up wherever a value fits — assignments, conditions, other calls.

options: Procedures return values and functions don't
Procedures do an action; functions compute and return a value
check.question: Procedure vs function, in one line:

screens.heading: Calling your own units
screens.keyPoint: Procedures act (own line). Functions answer (wherever a value fits).

screens.body: Let's see the whole skeleton working at once: declare variables, do the work, catch the failure. This block looks up a product's price, applies a discount, and if the product doesn't exist, falls back to 0 instead of crashing. Every piece you've learned, in one place.

options: It falls back to 0 via the EXCEPTION section
check.question: If product 999 doesn't exist, what happens?

screens.heading: The full block, all together
screens.keyPoint: DECLARE → BEGIN → EXCEPTION → END, working as one.

title: The Anatomy of a Database Block
